paragraphs: The paper presents a model of how people perceive multiple directions of motion and the aftereffects those motions produce. Its central problem is that two moving groups of dots can look like one combined movement or like two overlapping movements. Yet the aftereffect can appear as a single movement in either case.

The model uses two successive stages of direction-sensitive units. Units in the first stage respond to a relatively broad range of directions, while units in the second respond more narrowly. Adaptation occurs in the first stage, and inhibitory interactions occur in the second. These mechanisms jointly account for the motion aftereffect.

When the dot groups move in nearby directions, the model explains their perceptual combination into movement along the vector sum. When their directions differ substantially, it explains the perception of separate, transparent motions. Accounting for the single-motion aftereffect in both situations connects otherwise different perceptual experiences through the same two-stage architecture.
neurips-1995-a-model-of-transparent-moti.tldr: A two-stage motion model explains both overlapping motion perception and why its aftereffect appears as a single motion.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of optimizing neural networks whose behavior is governed by a general objective function. Practical objectives can have poor local extrema: solutions that look favorable nearby but are unsatisfactory overall. This makes the path taken by an optimization procedure important, particularly when the problem contains many variables.

The proposed framework combines deterministic annealing, multiscale optimization, attention mechanisms, and trust region methods. These bring together ways of changing the optimization landscape, working at different scales, directing computational effort, and controlling local optimization steps. The contribution is their combination into a framework intended for large optimization problems.

The abstract reports efficient minimization of objectives with thousands of variables. It also emphasizes that the framework assumes little about the objective and accommodates nonlinear, nonconvex functions. That scope matters because these functions need not have a single convenient minimum. The stated result supports combining complementary optimization techniques to handle difficult objectives, without implying that every resulting solution is globally optimal.
neurips-1995-a-multiscale-attentional-fr.tldr: A framework combining annealing, multiple scales, attention, and trust regions efficiently minimizes difficult objectives with thousands of variables.

paragraphs: The paper presents a practical method for training feedforward neural networks using Bayesian learning. The emphasis is on making this approach computationally usable and evaluating whether it helps on real prediction tasks. Its evaluation focuses on settings with limited data, where the training examples provide relatively little evidence about the network's parameters.

The method uses sophisticated Monte Carlo techniques to carry out Bayesian training. Monte Carlo methods use sampling to approximate calculations involving uncertainty. In this setting, they provide a computational route to learning with uncertainty about network parameters. The paper's central contribution is an implementation that makes this approach practical within the reported computing budget.

The abstract reports that the method outperformed other leading methods on five real-world tasks with limited data, while requiring reasonably small amounts of computer time. These findings connect predictive performance with computational feasibility. They provide evidence that Bayesian neural-network training can be useful in practical small-data settings, rather than leaving its value solely at the level of a statistical formulation.
neurips-1995-a-practical-monte-carlo-imp.tldr: Monte Carlo methods make Bayesian neural-network training practical and outperform competing methods on five real-world tasks with limited data.

paragraphs: The paper develops a regularizer for recurrent neural networks by starting with a desired property: predictions should remain reliable when the training data are perturbed. A regularizer adds a preference to the learning objective, steering training toward particular kinds of solutions. Here, that preference comes from robustness to changes in the data.

The resulting smoothing penalty extends the first-order Tikhonov stabilizer to dynamic models. The authors derive a closed-form expression covering both time-lagged recurrent networks and networks with simultaneous recurrence. Feedforward networks and single-layer linear networks fall within the same expression as special cases, giving the method a common mathematical basis across several architectures.

In the reported case studies, the regularizer performed better than standard quadratic weight decay. Weight decay directly penalizes large weights, while this derivation ties the penalty to prediction sensitivity. The comparison therefore supports the practical value of regularizing a network according to how its predictions respond to perturbations, including when recurrence makes those responses depend on dynamic interactions.
neurips-1995-a-smoothing-regularizer-for.tldr: A robustness-derived smoothing penalty covers several recurrent architectures and outperforms quadratic weight decay in reported case studies.

paragraphs: The paper proposes the Ying-Yang Machine as a shared mathematical framework for supervised and unsupervised learning. Its starting point is that a joint probability distribution has two complementary but equivalent Bayesian representations. The scheme builds a learning formulation around these representations and the Kullback divergence used to compare them.

This approach treats apparently different learning procedures as related instances of a broader construction. The abstract places maximum likelihood, least-squares learning, maximum information preservation, EM and em algorithms, information geometry, and the Helmholtz machine within that construction. The intended contribution is a common account of their underlying learning principles.

The framework is also presented as a source of new variants, results, and learning models. Its significance therefore has two parts: organizing existing methods and providing a basis for deriving additional ones. A common probabilistic formulation can make relationships among learning objectives easier to see. The stated contribution is this unification and model generation, rather than a reported performance comparison on a particular application.
neurips-1995-a-unified-learning-scheme-b.tldr: The Ying-Yang Machine uses complementary Bayesian representations and Kullback divergence to unify learning methods and derive new models.

paragraphs: The paper develops an active learning method specifically for multilayer perceptrons. Active learning concerns choosing informative training examples, so the usefulness of the selection rule depends on how well it describes the network being trained. The authors identify a mathematical obstacle affecting many selection methods based on Fisher information.

That obstacle is a singular information matrix. Such a matrix lacks the independent information needed for some of the calculations that information-based methods rely on. The authors derive the condition under which this singularity occurs in multilayer perceptrons, making the source of the problem explicit instead of assuming the matrix is always suitable.

Their proposed solution incorporates hidden-unit reduction into an active learning technique applicable to these networks. This connects the choice of training examples with the structure of the model itself: the network representation matters to whether the selection criterion works. The abstract reports experimental verification of the method's effectiveness, supporting the practical relevance of addressing singularity when designing active learning for multilayer perceptrons.
neurips-1995-active-learning-in-multilay.tldr: An active learning method uses hidden-unit reduction to address singular Fisher information matrices in multilayer perceptrons.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a mixture model for supervised learning of probabilistic transducers. A transducer represents a mapping from inputs to outputs, with probabilities describing uncertainty in that mapping. A mixture allows several such models to participate, making the learning problem include both the component models and their combination.

The authors devise an online algorithm that learns as examples arrive. It efficiently infers each component's structure as well as estimating its parameters. This distinction matters: estimating parameter values presumes a model structure, whereas learning structure also determines the form of the model used to explain the examples.

Theoretical analysis and comparative simulations indicate that the algorithm tracks the best model in an arbitrarily large, potentially infinite pool. This is a claim about adapting competitively among candidate models, rather than needing to settle on a small fixed collection beforehand. The paper also applies the approach to learning a noun phrase recognizer, connecting its general sequence-modeling formulation with a concrete language-processing task.
neurips-1995-adaptive-mixture-of-probabi.tldr: An online mixture algorithm learns probabilistic transducer structures and parameters while tracking the best model in a potentially infinite pool.

paragraphs: The paper presents a Bayesian way to infer the parameters of a mixture of experts. Such a model combines multiple component predictors, allowing different experts to contribute to its predictions. The learning problem is to determine the model's parameters while accounting for uncertainty in what the available observations support.

The proposed framework uses ensemble learning through variational free energy minimization. This supplies an optimization-based route to Bayesian inference, allowing the method to work with uncertainty over model parameters. Its purpose is to improve on traditional maximum likelihood inference, which the abstract identifies as vulnerable to overfitting and underestimating noise.

These two problems are related in practical interpretation: a model can fit observations too closely while treating their unexplained variation as smaller than it really is. The authors state that their Bayesian approach avoids both problems and demonstrate it on artificial tasks and sunspot time-series prediction. The contribution connects a probabilistic treatment of model uncertainty with more appropriate fitting and noise estimation in mixtures of experts.
neurips-1995-bayesian-methods-for-mixtur.tldr: Variational Bayesian learning addresses overfitting and underestimated noise in mixtures of experts.

paragraphs: The paper studies how online gradient descent changes a two-layer neural network over time. The network updates its weights after each independent training example, so the number of examples acts as a clock for the learning process. An analytic solution is used to investigate how the learning rate controls this evolution and its convergence.

The analysis uses a teacher-student setting. A teacher network defines the desired mapping, and a student network learns from examples of that mapping. Their numbers of hidden units may differ. Generalization error measures the disagreement between the student's learned function and the target, connecting weight dynamics to predictive ability.

The discussion is restricted to a soft-committee machine: hidden units have fixed positive output weights of one, and only input-to-hidden weights adapt. The hidden activation is an error function. These choices define the setting in which the analytic account is developed. The paper's contribution is to make the learning trajectory mathematically accessible, providing a way to examine how learning-rate choices influence progress toward the target function.
neurips-1995-dynamics-of-on-line-gradien.tldr: An analytic account of online learning examines how the learning rate shapes generalization and convergence in two-layer networks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the complexity of logical functions develops across a network. Two overlapping waves move through the network: one prunes connections, and the other reinforces them through Hebbian learning. The question is how this combination of connection removal and strengthening relates to the kinds of functions that appear.

The analysis distinguishes linearly separable functions from functions that are not linearly separable, using the network's two inputs. This distinction separates functions whose outputs can be divided by a linear boundary from those requiring a more complex division. The reported results show a significant spatial gradient in the appearance of both types.

Cells representing nonlinearly separable functions are much sparser. Moreover, the slope describing their appearance changes with model parameters in a strongly nonlinear way. Thus, the richer logical functions do not simply emerge uniformly throughout the network or vary proportionally with parameter changes. The findings connect the spatial organization of pruning and reinforcement with the distribution and sensitivity of computational complexity.
neurips-1995-explorations-with-the-dynam.tldr: Overlapping pruning and reinforcement waves produce spatial gradients in logical complexity, with sparse nonlinear functions showing strong parameter sensitivity.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether reinforcement learning can work reliably when function approximation is needed to generalize across continuous states. Earlier experiments had reported failures on several control problems. The authors revisit all of those tasks and add a substantially larger one, reporting positive results throughout their evaluation.

Two major differences distinguish their approach: they use sparse coarse coding through CMAC function approximators, and they learn online. Sparse coarse coding represents situations through a limited set of active features, allowing shared parameters to support generalization. The earlier work used mostly global approximators and offline learning, making representation and learning procedure central to the comparison.

The authors also test the suggestion that learning should rely on actual outcomes through rollouts, corresponding to the full-return setting of temporal-difference learning. In their experiments, this consistently performs substantially worse. The findings support using function approximation with reinforcement learning and challenge a blanket preference for full-return methods. They are empirical evidence of robust performance on these tasks, against a background of limited convergence theory.
neurips-1995-generalization-in-reinforce.tldr: Online reinforcement learning with sparse coarse coding succeeds on previously troublesome control tasks and outperforms full-return learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Generalized Learning Vector Quantization, or GLVQ, as a way to train reference vectors for recognition. Reference vectors serve as representative points used by the classifier. Moving them during learning changes how the classifier organizes its input space, so the update rule directly affects recognition performance.

GLVQ derives those movements from a cost function and uses steepest descent to reduce it. The cost is selected so that the resulting learning rule satisfies a convergence condition. This gives the updates an explicit optimization basis. The authors also prove that Kohonen's rule, as used in LVQ, fails to satisfy that condition and associate this failure with degraded recognition.

Experiments on printed Chinese character recognition show better recognition with GLVQ than with LVQ. The result connects the mathematical design of the update rule with a practical classification benefit. The paper's main contribution is therefore both a diagnosis of the existing rule and a replacement whose cost function is constructed to support convergence.
neurips-1995-generalized-learning-vector.tldr: GLVQ derives reference-vector updates from a convergence-compatible objective and improves printed Chinese character recognition over LVQ.

paragraphs: The paper develops a geometric theory of early stopping for linear models. Training is represented as gradient descent in continuous time, producing a trajectory from the initial weights toward the training set's least-squares solution. A validation set determines where along that trajectory training should stop.

The first result constrains the possible stopping weights: for given training and validation sets, they must lie on a particular quadric surface, usually an ellipsoid. A second result reverses the perspective. Given the training set and a candidate stopping vector, the least-squares solutions associated with validation sets that yield that stopping point lie on a particular plane.

This plane relationship provides a way to estimate the probability of stopping at different positions on the training trajectory. It also supports estimating the probability that training continues indefinitely. The contribution turns early stopping into a geometric and probabilistic object of study. The theory is developed for linear models, while possible extensions to nonlinear models are discussed.
neurips-1995-geometry-of-early-stopping-.tldr: A geometric theory characterizes early-stopping weights in linear models and supports estimating where training will stop.

paragraphs: The paper challenges a proposed mechanism for performing symbolic computation with connectionist networks. Harmony networks were claimed to construct valid parse trees for strings in a context-free language by settling into a stable equilibrium. The authors show that these networks also produce many outputs that are not valid parse trees.

The proposal connects several mathematical objects. A tensor representation interprets network activations as tree structures. A harmony function assigns zero precisely to valid trees and negative integers to invalid ones. Separately, an energy function is defined over network activations and minimized by the network. A recursive construction determines its weight matrix.

The key issue is whether these pieces ensure that the network's resulting output satisfies the symbolic rules. The reported invalid outputs show that the proposed construction does not deliver the claimed guarantee. This matters because successful energy minimization alone is insufficient if the resulting activation pattern fails to represent a valid parse. The criticism concerns this mechanism for symbolic computation, rather than establishing that connectionist systems cannot perform symbolic tasks.
neurips-1995-harmony-networks-do-not-wor.tldr: The paper shows that proposed harmony networks can produce invalid parse trees, undermining their claimed mechanism for symbolic parsing.

paragraphs: The paper studies neural networks for classifying airborne particles from laser-generated images. It contrasts this goal with environmental monitoring systems that assume particles are spherical and do not classify them. The proposed sensing approach produces two-dimensional scattering profiles, giving the classifier a pattern of measured light to analyze.

The authors compare template matching with two neural-network approaches, HyperNet and semi-linear units. All are evaluated as image classifiers for the scattering profiles. Template matching bases recognition on comparison with reference patterns; the neural-network alternatives learn a classification mapping. The comparison asks whether learned classifiers can provide useful recognition within this particle-monitoring setting.

The abstract reports that neural networks achieve recognition performance comparable to template matching while offering additional advantages. The central finding is therefore that the neural approach preserves useful classification capability in this application. By treating scattering profiles as images to recognize, the work connects laser-based particle sensing with learned pattern classification and moves beyond monitoring that relies only on a spherical-particle assumption.
neurips-1995-high-speed-airborne-particl.tldr: Neural networks classify laser scattering images of airborne particles with recognition performance comparable to template matching.

paragraphs: The paper compares two ways to improve how Gaussian mixture density estimates generalize beyond their training data. A Gaussian mixture models a probability distribution by combining Gaussian components. The concern is whether the fitted distribution captures patterns that carry over to other observations, making regularization a central part of the learning problem.

The first approach introduces a Bayesian prior over the model parameters. The authors derive expectation-maximization updates that maximize posterior parameter probability. This changes fitting from considering the observed data alone to also incorporating the preferences expressed by the prior. The result is a training procedure in which those preferences enter the parameter updates directly.

The second approach averages multiple density estimators, including through bagging. This places regularization at the level of combining fitted models instead of only modifying an individual model's objective. The paper brings these two approaches into a common comparison for density estimation, extending ensemble averaging beyond the classification setting highlighted in the abstract.
neurips-1995-improved-gaussian-mixture-d.tldr: The paper compares Bayesian parameter penalties and ensemble averaging as ways to improve Gaussian mixture density estimation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an algorithm for learning sparse perceptrons from representations containing high-order features. Such features allow a classifier to use combinations of input properties. Sparsity means that the final classifier relies on relatively few features, so a rich input representation need not lead to an equally complicated learned description.

The algorithm is based on hypothesis boosting. The authors establish that it can learn a particular class of target concepts in the probably approximately correct, or PAC, framework. This provides a formal learning guarantee for that class. The theoretical contribution concerns obtaining reliable learning while retaining a sparse perceptron representation.

Across three problem domains, the algorithm produces classifiers that use small numbers of features and generalize well. The authors also emphasize that the resulting concept descriptions are easy for people to understand. Together, these findings connect feature economy with prediction and interpretability: the selected features form both a working classifier and a compact description of what it has learned.
neurips-1995-learning-sparse-perceptrons.tldr: A boosting-based algorithm learns sparse perceptrons with theoretical guarantees and compact, understandable classifiers in three tested domains.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a difficulty in predicting protein structure from amino-acid sequences: beta sheets connect strands that can be far apart along the chain. Methods that examine only a small neighborhood around each amino acid do not directly capture these distant relationships. The authors introduce a network with two sequence windows to predict sheet structure.

After training on proteins, the network predicts sheets well but also produces many false positives. This makes local acceptance of every predicted pairing problematic. The method therefore combines its sheet predictions with a separate local prediction of three secondary-structure types: alpha helix, beta strand, and coil.

A global energy function brings these predictions together, and simulated annealing searches for a final assignment with low energy. This lets the final prediction reflect both distant strand relationships and local structural evidence. The contribution is a coordinated treatment of protein structure: the two-window network supplies nonlocal information, while global optimization reconciles that information with predictions about individual sequence regions.
neurips-1995-prediction-of-beta-sheets-i.tldr: A two-window network predicts distant beta-strand relationships, then global optimization combines them with local protein-structure predictions.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Probability Matching, an algorithm for associative reinforcement learning. Its central idea is to derive a probability distribution from the environment's reward signal and train a network so that its output probabilities match that distribution. Reward feedback thus becomes the basis for a probabilistic learning target.

The authors report that the algorithm learns faster and is less susceptible to local minima than previously existing algorithms. Local minima matter because training can settle into a solution that is hard to improve through nearby changes. The stated comparison suggests that the probability-matching formulation improves both learning speed and the reliability of finding useful solutions.

The method is also used to train mixtures of experts, an architecture for which other reinforcement learning rules reportedly fail to converge reliably even on simple problems. This architecture is a useful fit because it can represent complex functions while keeping output-probability calculation simple. The paper connects that computational convenience directly to the quantity its learning rule needs to match.
neurips-1995-reinforcement-learning-by-p.tldr: Probability Matching trains network output probabilities against reward-derived distributions, improving learning and enabling reliable mixture-of-experts training.

paragraphs: The paper introduces REMAP, a recursive approach to estimating and learning posterior probabilities. It develops the method for transition-based speech recognition, where neural networks provide probabilities for hidden Markov models. The overall task is to connect probabilities of local transitions with probabilities of complete word sequences.

REMAP uses local conditional posterior transition probabilities to estimate global posterior probabilities for word sequences. Its recursion resembles the expectation-maximization-based forward-backward procedure used for sequence likelihood estimation. The neural network's training targets are themselves estimates of local posterior probabilities, making the estimation of those targets part of the learning approach.

This formulation links local network training to the sequence-level probabilities that speech recognition ultimately requires. An initial experiment reports a significant reduction in error rate relative to a baseline system. The evidence therefore supports the approach in its presented speech-recognition setting, while the authors describe the underlying method as more general. The distinctive contribution is recursive posterior estimation coupled to training on estimated posterior targets.
neurips-1995-remap-recursive-estimation-.tldr: REMAP recursively estimates posterior probabilities to train speech-recognition networks and reduces error in an initial baseline comparison.

paragraphs: The paper studies how tactile training changes the cortical map representing the hand. Such maps organize sensory inputs spatially in the brain, and behavioral training can alter that organization. Earlier computer simulations had shown that competitive neural networks behave in ways consistent with these changes, motivating a more mathematical account.

The authors use Amari's neural field theory to model the hand representation in primate somatosensory cortex. They derive expressions for changes in receptive-field size and magnification factor. These describe two related aspects of the map: the extent of sensory input represented by a responding region and how much cortical representation is allocated to the sensory surface.

The derived changes agree with observations from owl monkey experiments. The model also makes a prediction extending beyond those observations. Its contribution is therefore more than reproducing a qualitative pattern of reorganization: it provides explicit relationships for measurable map properties. This connects a theory of interacting neural populations with how sensory representations change through training.
neurips-1995-reorganisation-of-somatosen.tldr: A neural field model derives training-related changes in cortical hand maps that agree with owl monkey observations and yield a further prediction.

paragraphs: SEEMORE is a neurally inspired system for recognizing familiar objects despite changes in viewing angle, distance, and nonrigid shape. Its database contains 100 objects spanning rigid, flexible, articulated, statistical, and complex examples. This range makes recognition involve more than matching a single unchanging shape from a fixed viewpoint.

The system uses 102 color and shape feature channels within a simple feedforward architecture. With a nearest-neighbor classifier, it correctly identifies 97% of 600 previously unseen test views, comprising six views of each object. Chance performance is 1%. The images are color video views presenting objects individually.

Comparable performance is reported for the subset of 15 nonrigid objects, supporting recognition across changes that go beyond rigid viewpoint transformations. The system's generalization also reveals natural category structure that was not explicitly encoded in the input feature dimensions. The findings show how combining multiple visual cues can support recognition of known objects and produce meaningful similarities among them.
neurips-1995-seemore-a-view-based-approa.tldr: SEEMORE combines color and shape cues to recognize 100 known objects with 97% accuracy across 600 novel views.

paragraphs: The paper extends a computational model of how motor endplates develop at the junction between nerves and muscles. Its focus is synaptic competition: how the connections involved in this organization persist or are lost. The proposed extension includes competition that depends on activity as well as competition that does not.

The model is motivated by neurophysiological evidence linking synaptic efficacy with synaptic survival. Efficacy concerns how effectively a connection functions, while survival concerns whether it remains present. Bringing both activity-dependent and activity-independent competition into the dual constraint model allows these influences to be considered within the same account of synaptic organization.

The authors provide a molecular justification for the computational model and report that its predictions match the behavior of real synapses during development and regeneration. Agreement in both settings matters because the model addresses the formation and reformation of connections. The contribution links functional effectiveness, competition, and biological mechanisms in an explanation of which synapses survive.
neurips-1995-the-role-of-activity-in-syn.tldr: An extended synaptic competition model combines activity-dependent and independent mechanisms to explain developmental and regenerative behavior.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to choose decision-tree splits that balances geometric flexibility with search cost. Conventional binary trees either use boundaries aligned with individual input axes or search the continuous space of freely oriented boundaries. The former restricts the available splits, while the latter can require expensive optimization.

The authors generate candidate boundaries directly from pairs of training points. For each pair, they use the hyperplane that passes through the midpoint and is perpendicular to the line joining the points. This produces a specific candidate from the geometry of the data, allowing boundaries with varied orientations without searching every possible orientation.

Across 12 datasets, this candidate-generation method outperforms the standard methods, particularly when training sets are small. The result suggests that the placement of observed examples can provide useful guidance for selecting flexible splits. The contribution is a concrete alternative search space for tree construction: pair-defined boundaries offer more geometric freedom than axis-aligned splits while avoiding an unrestricted continuous search.
neurips-1995-using-pairs-of-data-points-.tldr: Decision-tree splits defined by pairs of training points outperform standard approaches across 12 datasets, especially with small training sets.

paragraphs: The paper implements a one-dimensional model of primate smooth pursuit in CMOS VLSI hardware. Smooth pursuit aims to keep a moving target stable on the retina by matching eye movement to target movement. The model combines negative and positive feedback schemes to drive the target's retinal velocity toward zero.

The system also uses current eye motion to predict future target motion. For sensing at the focal plane, it employs a local correlation method to detect visual motion. The resulting velocity measurements supply the pursuit controller, linking motion detection with the feedback mechanism in a complete hardware system.

The reported velocity measurements span four orders of magnitude with less than 15% variation. The complete system successfully tracks velocity in high-contrast scenes. The paper also discusses stability, analysis, and correspondence with biology. Its contribution is a working connection between a biological control model and integrated-circuit implementation, with the high-contrast condition defining the stated setting for successful tracking.
neurips-1995-vlsi-model-of-primate-visua.tldr: A CMOS implementation combines visual motion sensing and feedback control to model smooth pursuit and track high-contrast motion.
